problem.heading:
A running pump can still
leave a service at risk.
problem.intro: Check the machine, the delivered service and the surrounding area—not just whether the motor is running.

cards.title: Mechanical changes between rounds
cards.body: A new vibration or housing-temperature pattern can justify a closer look. Use repeatable mounting points so a changed installation is not mistaken for a changed machine.

cards.title: Running does not mean delivering
cards.body: A run signal alone does not prove useful flow. Compare pressure, measured flow and electrical load before investigating supply loss, a valve position or a changed duty.

cards.title: Leaks outside the process
cards.body: Water can collect below pump seals, cooling lines or condensate trays while vibration remains normal. Place leak sensing where escaping water is likely to reach, then assign a named response.

problem.takeaway: Know which machine changed, whether it still delivers the required service, and where water needs attention.

focus.heading:
Measure the condition.
Verify the outcome.
focus.intro: Link each observation to a maintenance decision, and every remote command to independent feedback.

stages.title: Map the consequential risks
stages.body: Identify critical machines, water escape paths, supply limits and the service affected by an interruption.

stages.title: Measure at the right point
stages.body: Use rigid machine mounts, suitable process connections and leak probes at defined dry locations.

stages.title: Compare delivered service
stages.body: Bring in flow, run/fault, current or power records from compatible meters, drives and controls.

stages.title: Act and check the result
stages.body: Inspect the cause or issue a commissioned controller command, then confirm equipment state and service recovery.

focus.note: Overall condition trends guide investigation. Specific fault diagnosis and equipment protection require their own suitable methods.
focus.detailTitle: Why distinguish a command, a run signal and useful flow?
focus.detail: An output command records what was requested. A separate run/fault input or drive status reports equipment state, while a suitable flow meter shows the water delivered. Current alone does not measure real electrical power or prove hydraulic performance. Use approved interfaces and aligned timestamps to compare these records. For a remote action, define permissions, local/remote selection, start permissives, timeout handling and loss-of-communications behaviour. Existing machine protection and emergency stops remain local and effective.

cards.title: Building booster pump sets

cards.task: Track vibration, temperature and discharge pressure; add water-leak points beneath seals and connections.
cards.placement: Rigid motor points, approved process ports and normally dry floor or drip-tray locations.
cards.response: Investigate the affected unit and leak location; verify run/fault and measured delivery before returning it to service.

cards.title: Industrial circulation pumps
cards.alt: Industrial pump and motor serving a process-water circulation loop
cards.task: Compare vibration and temperature with pressure, measured flow and drive current or power.
cards.placement: Repeatable bearing points, process ports and compatible meter or drive interfaces.
cards.response: Distinguish a changed load from reduced delivery; confirm the cause before maintenance or an authorised operating change.

cards.title: Cooling-water & HVAC utilities
cards.alt: Cooling-water plant room with accessible pump and pipe installations
cards.task: Watch cooling-water leaks, condensate overflow, reserve level and the condition of circulation pumps.
cards.placement: Tray outlets, equipment bases and selected pipe routes; use separate level and temperature points.
cards.response: Locate the wet area, check drainage and supplies, and verify any commissioned isolation or pump command through feedback.

cards.title: Wastewater lift-station equipment
cards.alt: Water treatment pump equipment in an industrial service area
cards.task: Combine accessible pump vibration, wet-well level, run/fault status and an independent high-level contact where required.
cards.placement: Suitable machine and level points; approved contacts from the station control or protection system.
cards.response: Check duty/standby operation and local protection; investigate failed starts or rising water under the station procedure.

platform.heading:
From an exception
to a checked response.

steps.title: Find the affected point
steps.body: Identify the machine or wet zone, event time and data freshness before assigning the investigation.

steps.title: Respond through the agreed route
steps.body: Dispatch maintenance or issue an authorised command through the commissioned HD20 or compatible control interface.

steps.title: Verify service recovery
steps.body: Check run/fault or valve feedback, pressure and measured flow; retain the finding and action against the asset.

platform.boundary: Remote control uses a separately commissioned electrical interface and local protection. A cloud command acknowledgement is not proof that a motor ran or a valve moved.

faq.q: Which sensors are needed for Smart Equipment Monitoring?
faq.a: For pumps and motors, start with vibration, temperature and pressure. Add water-leak sensors at consequential dry locations, liquid level where supply or collection matters, and flow or electrical feedback where delivered service must be checked. The equipment risk and maintenance decision determine the combination; every sensor is not required on every machine.

faq.q: Where should water-leak sensors be installed, and can they detect oil?
faq.a: Place water-leak probes where escaped water is likely to reach: below pump seals or flanges, in normally dry drip trays, around cooling-water equipment and beside condensate routes. Test the actual water path and account for washdown or routine drainage. Water-contact detection does not identify the leak source or automatically detect oil, fuel or chemicals; those liquids need a separately selected sensing method and compatibility assessment.

faq.q: Can a vibration value identify a specific fault?
faq.a: An overall RMS trend shows a change to investigate. It does not uniquely distinguish imbalance, misalignment, looseness or other causes. Check comparable speed and load, mounting condition and related process measurements. Specialist diagnosis may need additional acquisition, spectra or other evidence beyond the supplied overall trend.

faq.q: Where should the vibration probe be installed?
faq.a: Use an approved rigid point near the relevant bearing and document its sensing direction. Avoid flexible covers and unverified adapters. For the external-probe arrangement, secure the cable and locate the wireless terminal where access, exposure limits and radio coverage are appropriate for the supplied assembly.

faq.q: Can current, flow and PLC status appear with the sensor data?
faq.a: Yes, through selected instruments and a defined interface. An HD20 IoT Controller can collect compatible status and analogue signals; supported serial equipment may use an appropriately configured HR10 interface. Confirm signal type, electrical limits, channel count, protocol, units and timestamps. A controller input does not replace the flow meter or current/power transducer that produces the measurement.

faq.q: Can Hitelecom remotely switch equipment or valves?
faq.a: A commissioned HD20 or compatible controller interface can support authorised commands to a pump starter, valve control or other suitable equipment. Select an interposing relay, contactor or actuator interface where the load requires it; do not assume a controller output can directly power a motor. Define local/remote selection, permissives, protection, command timeouts and independent run or end-position feedback. Remote monitoring and control do not replace the machine protection system.

faq.q: How should alarms and reporting intervals be set?
faq.a: Base them on the machine type, expected duty and time available to respond. Define acquisition separately from wireless reporting, and agree persistence and escalation with maintenance staff. Avoid one threshold or interval for every pump; verify the chosen configuration during representative operating conditions.

faq.q: Why add flow and electrical measurements to vibration?
faq.a: They help establish whether a running machine is delivering its intended service at a comparable duty. A suitable flow meter measures delivery; drive or current data adds load context; a power meter is needed when real electrical power or energy is the question. Compare these with pressure and temperature before assigning a fault. A single changed value does not uniquely diagnose dry running, blockage or leakage.
